```{r}
#| label: libraries
#| message: false
#| warning: false
library(brms)
library(bicountbrms)
library(posterior)  # summaries of the posterior draws
library(dplyr)      # data manipulation
library(ggplot2)    # the figure
```

In a partially paired design, one source has missing values: source 2 records
a count $y_2$ on every unit, and source 1 records a count $y_1$ on only some of
the units. Interest usually lies in estimating the congruence and the source
bias (see [Getting started][started] and
[*The congruence–bias parameterisation*][reparameterisation]), and in imputing
the missing values of $y_1$ from all the information available, including the
recorded values of $y_2$. Here, we simulate a partially paired design with two
treatments and show how to obtain these estimates and imputations from a model
fitted with `binegbin_partialobs()`.

## Structuring the data

The counts of the source that records every unit are the column `y2`, and
the counts of the other source are the column `y1`. The observation indicator
`y1_obs` is `1` on a paired row (where $y_1$ was recorded) and `0` on an
unpaired row (where $y_1$ is missing), and is passed to the family with $y_2$
as `vint(y2, y1_obs)`, in that order. An indicator other than `0` or `1` makes the sampler
fail at initialisation, with a message in the chain output. The same check
catches the two arguments of `vint()` written in reverse order. On an
unpaired row, `y1` can be any integer, because the likelihood term for that row
does not depend on `y1`. We suggest `-1`, because it cannot be confused with a
recorded count. **`y1` must not be `NA` on an unpaired row**, because brms
drops any row with a missing response before the likelihood is evaluated.

## Simulated design

The design has 10 groups, such as sites, and two treatments, `A` and `B`, with
30 units for each combination of group and treatment. The midpoint $M$ varies
among groups. The congruence and the source bias differ between treatments,
with $f = 0.6$ and $\beta = 0$ under treatment `A`, and $f = 0.85$ and
$\beta = 0.3$ under treatment `B`, so that under treatment `B` source 1 records
more exclusive events than source 2. Source 1 records $y_1$ on 18 of the 30 units (60%) in each
combination of group and treatment, and every simulated $y_1$ is kept in
`y1_true`, against which the imputation is checked.

```{r}
#| label: simulate
set.seed(4)

# The midpoint M varies among the 10 groups: log M is normal with mean log(5)
# and SD 0.4.
groups <- data.frame(
  group = factor(1:10),
  logM  = rnorm(10, log(5), 0.4)
)

# The congruence f and the source bias beta differ between the two treatments.
treatments <- data.frame(
  treatment = factor(c("A", "B")),
  f         = c(0.6, 0.85),
  beta      = c(0, 0.3)
)

# 30 units for each combination of group and treatment, 600 units in all.
design <- merge(
  merge(groups, treatments),
  data.frame(unit = 1:30)
)

# The native parameters on each unit. Every overdispersion is 0.5.
dpars <- with(
  design,
  mfd_to_dpars(
    M         = exp(logM),
    f         = f,
    delta     = atanh(beta),
    kappas    = 0.5,
    kappaxone = 0.5,
    kappaxtwo = 0.5
  )
)

# rbicount() draws y1, y2, and the latent counts Ns, N1, and N2 on each unit.
# Source 1 records y1 on 18 of the 30 units, chosen at random, in each
# combination of group and treatment. On the other units, y1 is missing, as in
# real data, and the simulated value is kept in y1_true.
dat <- cbind(design, do.call(rbicount, c(list(n = nrow(design)), dpars))) |>
  group_by(group, treatment) |>
  mutate(
    y1_true = y1,
    y1      = if_else(
      sample(rep(c(TRUE, FALSE), times = c(18, 12))),
      y1,
      NA_integer_
    )
  ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  as.data.frame()

head(dat, 10)
```

## The model

Before the fit, the observation indicator is added and the missing values of
$y_1$ are set to `-1`, as described in [Structuring the data](#structuring-the-data):

```{r}
#| label: prepare
# Add the indicator y1_obs, 1 where source 1 recorded y1, and set the missing
# values of y1 to -1, so that brms keeps those rows
dat <- dat |>
  mutate(
    y1_obs = as.integer(!is.na(y1)),
    y1     = if_else(is.na(y1), -1L, y1)
  )

# The number of paired (y1_obs = 1) and unpaired (y1_obs = 0) units in each
# treatment
count(dat, treatment, y1_obs)
```

The model is written with `bf_mfd()` as in [Getting started][started]. The
response is `y1 | vint(y2, y1_obs)`, and the constructor and its Stan code are
`binegbin_partialobs()` and `binegbin_partialobs_stanvars()`. The formula for
`logM` includes a group-level effect of `group`, and the formulas for `logitf`
and `delta` include `treatment`, with one coefficient for each treatment.

```{r}
#| label: fit
#| eval: !expr has_stan
#| results: hide
#| message: false
fit <- brm(
  bf_mfd(
    y1 | vint(y2, y1_obs),           # the indicator y1_obs follows y2
    logM      ~ 1 + (1 | group),     # M varies among groups
    logitf    ~ 0 + treatment,       # one congruence for each treatment
    delta     ~ 0 + treatment,       # one source bias for each treatment
    kappas    ~ 1,
    kappaxone ~ 1,
    kappaxtwo ~ 1
  ),
  family   = binegbin_partialobs(),
  stanvars = binegbin_partialobs_stanvars(),
  data     = dat,
  # The priors of Getting started, with a prior on the SD of the group-level
  # effect on logM
  prior    = c(
    prior(normal(1.5, 1), class = "b",  nlpar = "logM"),
    prior(normal(0, 1),   class = "sd", nlpar = "logM"),
    prior(normal(0, 1.5), class = "b",  nlpar = "logitf"),
    prior(normal(0, 0.5), class = "b",  nlpar = "delta"),
    prior(normal(0, 1),   class = "b",  nlpar = "kappas",    lb = 0),
    prior(normal(0, 1),   class = "b",  nlpar = "kappaxone", lb = 0),
    prior(normal(0, 1),   class = "b",  nlpar = "kappaxtwo", lb = 0)
  ),
  chains  = 4,
  cores   = 4,
  iter    = 3000,
  refresh = 0,
  backend = "cmdstanr",  # or "rstan"
  seed    = 1
)
```

An unpaired row contributes the probability of $y_2$ alone, which does not
depend on the exclusive rate $\lambda_1$ or the overdispersion $\kappa_{x1}$ of
source 1. $\lambda_1$ and $\kappa_{x1}$ are therefore identified by the paired
rows alone. The congruence and the source bias are functions of $\lambda_1$,
so neither can be estimated without paired rows.
Where paired rows are few, the priors on `logitf`, `delta`, and `kappaxone` have
the most influence on the posterior.

Including the unpaired rows is valid if $y_1$ is missing at random given the
model: whether source 1 recorded a unit may depend on $y_2$ and on the
predictors, but not otherwise on $y_1$.

Where there is no reason to expect the two exclusive components to differ in
overdispersion, replacing `kappaxone ~ 1` and `kappaxtwo ~ 1` with the single
formula `kappax ~ 1` gives the two exclusive components one overdispersion,
which is informed by the unpaired rows as well as the paired rows.

## Recovery of the generating values

The table gives the posterior median and 95% credible interval of the
congruence and the source bias under each treatment, the overdispersion of the
exclusive component of source 1, and the SD of the group-level effect on
$\log M$, with the values that generated the counts.

```{r}
#| label: recovery
#| eval: !expr has_stan
# The values that generated the counts
truth <- c(
  f_A       = 0.6,
  f_B       = 0.85,
  beta_A    = 0,
  beta_B    = 0.3,
  kappaxone = 0.5,
  sd_logM   = 0.4
)

# Each parameter on its natural scale, summarised and compared with its true
# value
recovery <- as_draws_df(fit) |>
  mutate_variables(
    f_A       = plogis(b_logitf_treatmentA),
    f_B       = plogis(b_logitf_treatmentB),
    beta_A    = tanh(b_delta_treatmentA),
    beta_B    = tanh(b_delta_treatmentB),
    kappaxone = b_kappaxone_Intercept,
    sd_logM   = sd_group__logM_Intercept
  ) |>
  subset_draws(variable = names(truth)) |>
  summarise_draws(
    est = median,
    ~ quantile2(.x, probs = c(0.025, 0.975))
  ) |>
  mutate(
    truth   = truth[variable],
    covered = truth >= q2.5 & truth <= q97.5
  )

knitr::kable(recovery, digits = 2)
```

`r if (exists("recovery")) paste(if (all(recovery$covered)) "All six" else paste(sum(recovery$covered), "of the six"), "95% intervals contain the true value.")`

## Imputation of the missing values

`posterior_predict_y1_given_y2()` draws $y_1$ on each row from its distribution
given the recorded $y_2$, once for each posterior draw. `posterior_predict()`
draws $y_1$ from its marginal distribution, which depends on the predictors
alone. The two predictions are compared below with the values of $y_1$ withheld
from the model on the unpaired units.

```{r}
#| label: impute
#| eval: !expr has_stan
# Draws of y1 given y2, and marginal draws of y1: one row per posterior draw and
# one column per unit
y1_given_y2 <- posterior_predict_y1_given_y2(fit)
y1_marginal <- posterior_predict(fit)

# The unpaired units, on which y1 was withheld from the model
unpaired <- which(dat$y1_obs == 0)

# The posterior median and 90% interval of a prediction on each unpaired unit
summarise_prediction <- function(draws, prediction) {
  data.frame(
    dat[unpaired, c("treatment", "y1_true")],
    prediction = prediction,
    est        = apply(draws[, unpaired], 2, median),
    q5         = apply(draws[, unpaired], 2, quantile, 0.05),
    q95        = apply(draws[, unpaired], 2, quantile, 0.95)
  )
}

imputed <- rbind(
  summarise_prediction(y1_given_y2, "given y2"),
  summarise_prediction(y1_marginal, "marginal")
)

# The root mean square error of the posterior median, the mean width of the 90%
# interval, and the proportion of withheld values inside the interval
imputation_summary <- imputed |>
  summarise(
    rmse     = sqrt(mean((est - y1_true)^2)),
    width    = mean(q95 - q5),
    coverage = mean(y1_true >= q5 & y1_true <= q95),
    .by      = c(treatment, prediction)
  ) |>
  arrange(treatment, prediction)

knitr::kable(imputation_summary, digits = 2)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-imputation
#| eval: !expr has_stan
#| fig.width: 8
#| fig.height: 3.8
#| fig.cap: >
#|   Predictions of $y_1$ on the 240 unpaired units against the values of $y_1$
#|   withheld from the model, given the recorded $y_2$ (left) and from the
#|   marginal distribution of $y_1$ (right). Each point is the posterior median
#|   of the prediction for one unit, and each vertical line its 90% interval.
#|   The points are jittered horizontally, because the withheld values are
#|   integers. The dashed line marks equality of the prediction and the
#|   withheld value.
#| fig.alt: >
#|   Two scatterplots of predicted against withheld y1 for the unpaired units,
#|   coloured by treatment. Given y2, the points lie along the line of
#|   equality. The marginal predictions lie in horizontal bands at the mean of
#|   y1 for each group and treatment.
imputed |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(
    x      = y1_true,
    y      = est,
    ymin   = q5,
    ymax   = q95,
    colour = treatment
  ) +
  geom_abline(
    slope     = 1,
    intercept = 0,
    linetype  = 2,
    colour    = "grey50"
  ) +
  geom_linerange(
    position = position_jitter(width = 0.25, height = 0, seed = 1),
    alpha    = 0.35
  ) +
  geom_point(
    position = position_jitter(width = 0.25, height = 0, seed = 1),
    size     = 1.2
  ) +
  facet_wrap(
    ~ prediction,
    labeller = as_labeller(
      c(
        "given y2" = "Predicted y1 conditional on y2",
        "marginal" = "Predicted y1 marginal"
      )
    )
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(A = "#2D6A7F", B = "#C4622D")) +
  labs(
    x      = "Withheld y1",
    y      = NULL,
    colour = "Treatment"
  ) +
  theme_bw()
```

```{r}
#| label: imputation-numbers
#| include: false
# Quoted in the prose below, so that the text tracks the fit. The summary
# exists only where the fitting chunks ran.
imp_at <- function(tr, pr, col) {
  if (!exists("imputation_summary")) return(NA)
  x <- imputation_summary[[col]][
    imputation_summary$treatment == tr & imputation_summary$prediction == pr
  ]
  sprintf("%.1f", x)
}
```

The root mean square error of the posterior median of $y_1$ was smaller for
the prediction given $y_2$ than for the marginal prediction:
`r imp_at("A", "given y2", "rmse")` against `r imp_at("A", "marginal", "rmse")`
under treatment `A`, and `r imp_at("B", "given y2", "rmse")` against
`r imp_at("B", "marginal", "rmse")` under treatment `B`. The 90% intervals of
the prediction given $y_2$ were also narrower than the 90% intervals of the
marginal prediction, with a mean width of `r imp_at("A", "given y2", "width")`
against `r imp_at("A", "marginal", "width")` under treatment `A`, and
`r imp_at("B", "given y2", "width")` against `r imp_at("B", "marginal", "width")`
under treatment `B`.
The advantage of the prediction given $y_2$, in root mean square error and in
interval width, is larger under treatment `B`, where the congruence is higher.
The predictions given $y_2$ are pulled towards the mean of $y_1$ for each
group and treatment, because the exclusive count of source 1 is independent of
$y_2$.

## Checks on the paired rows

On an unpaired row, `y1` is not a recorded count. `pp_check()`, `bayes_R2()`,
and `loo_R2()` compare predictions with `y1`, so for a partially paired fit,
these three functions should be run with `newdata` restricted to the paired
rows, as in `pp_check(fit, newdata = subset(dat, y1_obs == 1))`. `loo()`
needs no such restriction, because the likelihood term for an unpaired row does
not depend on `y1`. [Prediction and imputation][prediction] describes the
prediction functions and the brms functions for post-processing.
